title: 1 Corinthians 11:17–26
context: Paul now has no praise for them. Their gatherings for the Lord’s Supper do more harm than good, because divisions along social lines mean that some go hungry while others get drunk. Paul reminds them of what he received from the Lord and delivered to them: on the night he was betrayed, Jesus took bread and the cup, saying that the bread is his body and the cup the new covenant in his blood, to be done in remembrance of him. Whenever they eat and drink, they proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Both traditions treasure this passage. Arminian readers, especially Wesleyans, often call the Supper a converting as well as confirming ordinance; Reformed readers stress the Supper as a sign and seal of the covenant for believers.

verses.text: But in giving you this command, I don’t praise you, that you come together not for the better but for the worse.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul gives no praise, because their gatherings do more harm than good. Arminian readers see that the way believers treat one another affects whether worship pleases God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same. Outward observance of the sacrament does not please God when love and unity are absent.

verses.text: For first of all, when you come together in the assembly, I hear that divisions exist among you, and I partly believe it.
verses.arminianNotes: When they come together there are divisions, and Paul partly believes it. Arminian readers see divisions as a serious failure of love within the church.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see divisions as contrary to the unity the Supper signifies, a point Paul made in 10:17. A divided table contradicts the one bread.

verses.text: For there also must be factions among you, that those who are approved may be revealed among you.
verses.arminianNotes: There must be factions, so that the approved may be made known. Arminian readers see conflict as a test that reveals who is truly faithful.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s providence using even divisions to reveal genuine believers. The divisions remain sinful, yet God overrules them for the good of his church.

verses.text: When therefore you assemble yourselves together, it is not the Lord’s supper that you eat.
verses.arminianNotes: When they come together, it is not the Lord’s Supper they eat. Arminian readers see Paul’s strong judgment that their conduct empties the meal of its meaning.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see that the Supper requires the right use as well as the right words. Without love it is not truly the Lord’s table.

verses.text: For in your eating each one takes his own supper first. One is hungry, and another is drunken.
verses.arminianNotes: Each goes ahead with his own supper, one hungry and another drunk. Arminian readers see social and economic divisions dishonoring the poor among them.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same. Calvin noted that the Lord’s Supper should express a shared fellowship, not a private meal.

verses.text: What, don’t you have houses to eat and to drink in? Or do you despise God’s assembly, and put them to shame who don’t have enough? What shall I tell you? Shall I praise you? In this I don’t praise you.
verses.arminianNotes: Do they not have houses to eat in? Do they despise the church and shame those who have nothing? Arminian readers see special care for the poor as essential to the church’s life. The wealthy were treating the Lord’s table as their private banquet.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see contempt for the poor as contempt for the church of God. The church belongs to God, and how it is treated reflects on him.

verses.text: For I received from the Lord that which also I delivered to you, that the Lord Jesus on the night in which he was betrayed took bread.
verses.arminianNotes: Paul received from the Lord what he delivered: on the night of his betrayal, Jesus took bread. Arminian readers see the Supper’s authority resting on Christ’s own institution.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the words of institution as the foundation for the sacrament. The Reformed churches insist that the Supper be administered according to Christ’s institution and no additions.

verses.text: When he had given thanks, he broke it, and said, “Take, eat. This is my body, which is broken for you. Do this in memory of me.”
verses.arminianNotes: Jesus gave thanks, broke the bread, and said, This is my body, which is broken for you; do this in remembrance of me. Arminian readers see remembrance as a living, faith-filled recalling of Christ’s death, not mere memory, and Wesley taught that it was a means of grace.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see in “for you” the personal application of Christ’s death to believers. Remembrance is joined to real communion with Christ by the Spirit, as Calvin taught.
verses.keyContrast: Both traditions reject a bare memorial reading in their mainstream forms. Wesleyan Arminians see a means of grace that can even bring sinners to faith. Reformed readers see a sign and seal that nourishes those already united to Christ.

verses.text: In the same way he also took the cup, after supper, saying, “This cup is the new covenant in my blood. Do this, as often as you drink, in memory of me.”
verses.arminianNotes: The cup is the new covenant in his blood. Arminian readers see the new covenant offered to all who come in faith.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the new covenant of Jeremiah 31, which God will surely fulfill in his people. Reformed theology often links this to a definite atonement that secures the covenant blessings.

verses.text: For as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes.
verses.arminianNotes: As often as they eat and drink, they proclaim the Lord’s death until he comes. Arminian readers see the Supper as a proclamation of the gospel to all present.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the Supper as a visible word that proclaims Christ’s death. It looks back to the cross and forward to his return.
